newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FOCUS-Bulgarian lev slumps as C bank halts sales.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bulgarian lev slumps as C bank halts sales.

text.p: The Bulgarian lev slumped nearly 18 percent to record lows against the dollar on Wednesday as the central bank said it would stop intervening in the market and save its dollars to avert default on the country's foreign debt.
The lev closed at 335 to the dollar on the interbank market, plunging from Tuesday's close of 285 after foreign currency supply thinned to a trickle.

"The BNB will not react on the tension on the domestic forex market and spend its reserves (for interventions) because it must be prepared to meet pending foreign debt payments and the possible introduction of a currency board," said a Bulgarian National Bank official who asked not to be named.

Central bank foreign exchange reserves fell to $541 million at the end of October from $1.43 billion a year ago. Debt markets analysts speculated that Bulgaria could become the first country to default on a Brady debt restructuring deal.
Named after former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, the 1989 Brady plan provided help to highly indebted nations.
Payments of $300 million on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt fall due in the first quarter of 1997. The central bank also manages gold reserves worth some $400 million.

As Bulgarians rushed to turn their savings into dollars, the head of the State Savings Bank, Bistra Dimitrova, said panicked depositors had withdrawn 13 billion levs ($38.8 million) since the middle of last week and deposited 2.5 billion, making a net withdrawal of 10.5 billion.

"If the central bank really stops intervening on the interbank forex market in support of the lev, I expect another wave of panic among depositors, but I don't think the crisis of the last few days will happen again," she told Reuters.
The State Savings Bank, Bulgaria's largest savings institution, has so far been spared the liquidity problems affecting other banks.
Politicians and bankers are discussing an International Monetary Fund (IMF) proposal to introduce a currency board to stabilise the economy and halt the fall in the lev.

"We need to speed up discussions among parliamentary parties and to settle on a definite opinion on the measures needed for macro-economic stabilisation," Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov told reporters.

The IMF has expressed concern that corruption is blocking implementation of reforms in Bulgaria. Parliament's commission against corruption last week issued a White Book which blamed uncontrolled siphoning of funds abroad.

The cabinet has proposed operating a currency board that would stabilise the currency from the central bank by dividing it into two departments. One part would act as a currency board and the other as a banking department.

The proposal has raised fears over sovereignty and Bulgarian National Bank governor Lyubomir Filipov has said that under its statutes he could not support a currency board if it ruled out the existence of the central bank.
Under the system, the amount of national currency in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves, preventing the bank from printing money.
The question of who should run the board and how much independence it will be allowed has attracted even more speculation than the likely exchange rate at which the lev will be pegged.
Currency boards, usually pegging the local currency to the dollar, have been used by countries like Argentina, Estonia and Lithuania to restore confidence and defeat hyperinflation.
However, the opposition Union of Democratic Forces has said it will not support a currency board while the Socialists remain in power.
Once a consensus is reached, the proposal must be approved by parliament, where Videnov's Socialists have a majority. ($1=335 Leva)
